holding: In the wake of above discussion, we are of the firm view that there was no justification apparently available to the learned Tribunal to modify the quantum of punishment awarded by the Competent Authority in the case, therefore, the CPLA.No.851-L/2024 is converted into an appeal and allowed. As a consequence thereof, the impugned order of the learned Tribunal dated 08.12.2023 is set aside and the penalty for forfeiture of past service of 05 years imposed by the Secretary, Government of Punjab Special Education Department, Lahore vide order dated 15.02.2022 is restored and the service appeal filed by the respondent/petitioner in the learned Tribunal is dismissed. So far as the CPLA.No.1379-L/2024 filed by the petitioner/respondents is concerned, it is otherwise barred by 174 days. Since the Government’s appeal against the same order is allowed and punishment awarded by the department has been restored therefore, this civil petition is dismissed and leave is refused.

paragraphs.text: Muhammad Ali Mazhar, J: These Civil Petitions for leave to appeal are directed against the order dated 08.12.2023 passed by the Punjab Service Tribunal, Lahore (Tribunal) in Service Appeal No.4212/2022.

The short and snappy facts of the case are that the respondent in CP.851-L/2024 who is also the petitioner in CP.1379-L/2024 while serving as Principal/Headmistress (BS- 17) at Government Special Education Centre, Lyalpur Town, Faisalabad was issued show cause notice and statement of allegations under the provisions of the Punjab Employees Efficiency, Discipline & Accountability Act 2006 (PEEDA Act) on the following arraignments: i. "That due to inefficiency of the accused officer, Mr. Kamran Khan, Special Therapist (BS-17), Govt. Special Education Centre, Lyalpur Town, Faisalabad was living illegally in a room of the Centre without getting deduction of house rent allowance from the concerned District Account Officer, causing pecuniary loss to the government exchequer; ii. That the accused officer, being the Incharge and Supervisory Officer, failed to perform her duties efficiently and diligently and committed grave negligence and inefficiency and as result, Mr. Kamran Khan, Speech Therapist (BS-17) was in the habit of molesting the female teachers by blackmailing them, forcefully inducing them to have illicit relations with him and threatening them of dire consequences, which affected the atmosphere of the institution badly and hence, the institution became in- conducive for imparting education. Furthermore, Ms. Sadaf Arbab JSET was found absent from her duty for the last ten days but the accused officer never submitted her absence report nor reported high ups about the ill happening committed by Mr. Kamran Khan in the institution." [Emphasis applied] The Tribunal partly allowed the service appeal of the respondent and modified the penalty of forfeiture of past service for the period of five years to penalty of forfeiture of past service for one year.

The learned Additional Advocate General Punjab argued that while passing the impugned order, the learned Tribunal failed to appreciate that the respondent was found guilty of the charges and being the Incharge of the institution, failed to perform her administrative and supervisory role and committed grave negligence and inefficiency. It was further contended that the Competent Authority had already taken a lenient view and instead of dismissal from service, imposed the punishment of forfeiture of past service for a period of five years which did not deserve any further modification by the Tribunal. It was further averred that the respondent failed to vindicate her stance and prove her innocence, therefore, after considering all the aspects of the case, penalty was imposed in accordance with law and rules. He further argued that the respondent had no authority to grant permission to Kamran Khan, Speech Therapist, to live in the Institute illegally and get all the benefits including conveyance allowance and house rent with the connivance of the respondent. Furthermore, it was on record of regular inquiry that Kamran Khan, Speech Therapist, was in the habit of molesting the female teachers by blackmailing them, forcefully inducing them to have illicit relations with him and threatening them of dire consequences, which affected the atmosphere of the institution badly but no action was taken by the respondent on the complaints lodged to her by the female teachers.

The learned counsel for the respondent as well as the petitioner in CP.1379-l/2024, argued that the impugned order of the Tribunal modifying the punishment rather than giving a clean slate to the respondent is against the law and facts of the case. He further argued that in the de novo proceedings, the inquiry officer was inimical. It was further argued that the atmosphere of the institute was cordial as the respondent/petitioner not receive any complaint therefore, it could not be assumed that she failed to perform her obligations. It was further averred that during inquiry, no incriminatory evidence was brought on record against which it could be suggested that the respondent/petitioner committed any act or omission which could be treated as misconduct.

Heard the arguments. The astuteness of establishing Service Tribunals under Article 212 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 is to exclusively deal and decide the matters relating to the terms and conditions of service of civil servants and has same powers as vested in Civil Courts being a first fact-finding judicial forum. No doubt the employer/competent authority has the unqualified dominion to decide the quantum of punishment after due process in case of proven misconduct but this prerogative should be in line with the penalties and punishments provided under the law. The Courts and Tribunals under the power of judicial review may examine whether the punishment is proportionate or disproportionate vis-à-vis the proven guilt but this should be with proper application of mind and taking account of the gravity of charges and proof of guilt in the departmental inquiry but there is no untrammelled freedom of choice that in all circumstances, the quantum of punishment should be modified without justifying the mitigating circumstances. As opposed to structuring the verdict alone on the whims that “punishment seems to be harsh”, the learned Tribunal ought to examine the inquiry report and findings to ensure substantial justice which can be possible after vetting the entire material on record for awarding the clean chit or confirming or reducing the penalty.

In the case at hand, lamentably the learned Tribunal failed to fathom out that the allegations were of serious nature; the regular inquiry was conducted properly; female teachers appeared and deposed against the respondent/petitioner; fair right of cross-examination was afforded but the witnesses remained consistent with to their testimony and their evidence could not be shattered. The de novo inquiry report was based on oral as well documentary evidence. In case of serious allegations, the responsible person cannot be let free or exonerated with a low degree of penalty. If such gratuitous leniency is shown in obnoxious and repulsive matters, it will amount to lending a license to take up again alike acts in the future without any deterrence or trepidation. The department had already taken a lenient view and instead of dismissal or removal from service, awarded penalty of forfeiture of past service for the period of five years but the Tribunal very benevolently converted the penalty of forfeiture of past service for one year on the justification that the actual culprit was Kamran Khan without realizing the responsibilities and role of the respondent/petitioner as Headmistress of the educational institution.

By and large, in Latin language, the educational institutions are defined as “alma mater” which means "nourishing mother”, therefore it is always regarded as a venerated place of education and knowledge which primarily silhouettes the person’s career, intellectual and professional individuality and personality as a nourishing or fostering mother which obviously deserves a lifetime reverence by every pupil and alumnus for the institution that nurtured their personal and academic growth. The axiom “alma mater” commonly emblematizes a school, college, or university that a person attended and graduated from which also carries a sense of pride, affection, and respect. An educational institution is not merely a site of pure academic or commercial activity. Rather, it is increasingly recognized as a social and moral environment in which the dignity, autonomy, and safety of individuals must be protected, especially women, particularly in institutions where power hierarchies and reputational sensitivities silence victims and embolden perpetrators.

The most significant global instrument in this regard is the International Labour Organization’s Convention No. 190 on Violence and Harassment in the World of Work. The Convention recognizes “the right of everyone to a world of work free from violence and harassment” and imposes affirmative obligations upon employers to prevent, investigate, and remedy such conduct. The Convention further recognizes that women are disproportionately affected because of structural inequalities and entrenched power imbalances. In the case of Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (AIR 1997 SC 3011), the Indian Supreme Court recognized that women cannot participate equally in professional life where intimidation and abuse remain unchecked. Similarly, the Supreme Court of the United States in Meritor Savings Bank v. Vinson (477 U.S. 57) recognized sexual harassment as a form of sex discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act. The Court acknowledged that a hostile working environment itself may constitute unlawful discrimination even where no economic injury is immediately apparent. In the United Kingdom, the House of Lords in Majrowski v. Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Trust (2006 UK HL 34) affirmed that employers may bear legal responsibility where workplace harassment is tolerated within institutional structures, reflecting an evolving understanding that institutions themselves can perpetuate abuse through indifference or inaction.

The teachers and junior staff members often fear professional retaliation, reputational damage, or social ostracism if they complain against senior male colleagues but in this case, it is evident from record that the various complaints were lodged to the respondent (headmistress of the institution), who being a head of the institution should have played the role of “materfamilias” which refers to the mother of a family or the female head of a household or as “grande dame”, a French term meaning great lady, and refers to a woman who is highly respected, influential, and experienced, usually holding a position of prestige within a specific field, industry, or society. Being the Headmistress, the respondent was the chief administrator and was accountable for overall administration including the academic standards of teaching, learning, monitoring and controlling the safe and healthy working environment at the workplace as her utmost and dominant duty and she could not shut her eyes or behave quietly being tight-lipped on the complaints filed by the lady teachers for sexual harassment in writing against Kamran Khan. An institution that tolerates harassment fundamentally contradicts this educational mission because it teaches students that power excuses misconduct and silence is preferable to truth.

The sexual harassment of female teachers by male colleagues in any educational institution is a grave transgression and illegal behaviour and also a violation of law, ethics, and workplace dignity and self-respect, including unsolicited comments/ remarks, jokes, or messages of a sexual nature; catcalling or alike inappropriate behaviour; pressure for illicit favours in exchange for job benefits; attempts of unsolicited physical contact and creating hostile or unsafe work environment. Such acts and behavior not only violate a person’s dignity and safety but they also deteriorate the environment of the entire institution and creates an insecure and precarious environment at the workplace for the female teachers, hampering their professional abilities to impart education to the students with proper application of mind and required skills.

In order to fool proof a healthy environment at the workplace even in all the institutions where both male and female teachers are inducted and perform their duties, there must be an internal clear-headed harassment policy with proper reporting system to the high-ups, including the head of educational institution so that a fair investigation may be conducted against the delinquent and if the allegation is proved after due process of law, then disciplinary action may be taken against any such person who was found indulging in such nefarious and immoral activities, which should be done independently at departmental level and must not always be based or found awaiting the outcome of the decision if any rendered by the Federal Ombudsperson or Provincial Ombudsman for protection against harassment of women at the workplace. The head of the institution has an onerous duty to create such an environment at the workplace which should openly express and convey unequivocally for all that no sexual harassment would be acceptable at the workplace, rather professionalism with full dedication must be the set standard.

Sanguine to the gravity of the matter under discussion, the internationally-acclaimed best practices are also in existence in order to provide several essential safeguards such as confidential complaint channels, impartial inquiry committees, protection against retaliation, and mandatory timelines for investigation, psychological support for complainants, and visible disciplinary action against offenders. Along similar lines and being mindful to the importance of protection against harassment of women at the workplace, the Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010 is already in field wherein the expression “harassment” has been defined as unwelcome sexual advance, requests for sexual favours or other verbal or written communications or physical conduct of a sexual nature or sexually demeaning attitudes, causing interference with work performance or creating an intimidating, hostile or offensive work environment, or the attempt to punish the complainant for refusal to comply with such a request or is made a condition for employment; whereas the “workplace” means the place of work or the premises where an organization or employer operates and includes building, factory, open area or a larger geographical area where the activities of the organization or of the employer are carried out and includes any situation that is linked to official work or official activity outside the office. In order to ensure the protection against harassment, the aforesaid laws also mandate the formation of Inquiry Committee in each organization to enquire into the complaints by a Committee consisting of three members of whom at least one member shall be a woman. Finally, an office of “Ombudsperson” has been created to enquire into a complaint with an option to any employee either to prefer a complaint to the Ombudsperson or to the Inquiry Committee. Each employer has been made responsible to ensure implementation of the law including but not limited to incorporate the Code of Conduct for protection against harassment at the workplace as a part of their management policy and to form Inquiry Committee and management shall display copies of the Code in English as well as in the language understood by the majority of employees at a conspicuous place in the organization and the work place. In the Schedule of aforesaid laws, a Code of Conduct for Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace is also appended as a guideline for behaviour of all employees, including management, and the owners of an organization to ensure a work environment free of harassment and intimidation.

In tandem, the Principles and Purposes of the Higher Education Commission Policy on Protection against Harassment in Higher Education Institutions inter alia proclaims that Higher Education Institutions are highly consequential institutions in a society that are dedicated to the pursuit and dissemination of knowledge. It further explicates that protection against harassment is important not only because it threatens the freedom and conduciveness of the environment at institutions of higher learning, but at a more fundamental level, such conduct is unacceptable because it violates personal dignity and shall not be tolerated, under any circumstance. The goal of this policy is to prevent harassment at the working place, and where necessary to act upon complaints of harassment promptly, fairly, judiciously therefore, all administrators, deans, managers, faculty, department chairs, directors of schools or programs and others in supervisory or leadership positions have an obligation to be familiar with and to uphold this policy and its procedures along with informing members of their staff about its existence. The aforesaid policy was enacted pursuant to the Higher Education Commission Ordinance, 2002 and made binding on all higher education institutions in the country, whether operating in the public or private sectors and said to be consistent with and has been made in light of the provisions of the Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010. Even in this Policy document, under the nomenclature of “Prohibited Conduct”, “Harassment” means any unwelcome advance, request for favours or other verbal or written communication or physical conduct of a nature, or demeaning attitudes, where: a) Submission to such conduct is made either explicitly or implicitly a term or condition of an individual participation in any activity at the HEI; b) Submission to or rejection of such conduct by an individual is used as basis for academic or employment decision affecting that individual; or c) Such conduct has the purpose or effect of interfering with an individual’s academic or work performance, or of creating an intimidating, hostile, or offensive educational or working environment.

Whereas in clause 2.2 of the aforesaid policy manuscript, it is further provided that harassment may be overt or subtle and can range from visual signals or gestures to verbal abuse and physical contact along with hand/sign language to denote activity, persistent and unwelcome flirting, besides that in its “Annex 1”, various examples of manifestations (Actual Reported Cases) are jotted down. In addition, according to policy, some other behaviours are also prohibited, including a) Egregious Non-Consensual Acts: Acts that would be included in the category of attempted rape. While such situations will be covered under the laws of the country, and law enforcement institutions and the courts will investigate and adjudicate accordingly, the HEI administration has a special obligation to take preventative measures, offer immediate assistance and take interim measures when required; b) Non-Consensual Contact: Includes contact with another person without consent; c) Exploitation: Taking actions that violate the sexual privacy of others or taking sexual advantage of another without their consent. For example, taking pictures, videotaping, viewing or distributing explicit images or sexual information of another person without their consent; d) Pervasive or Severe Behaviours: It is not necessary that there be actual contact for a behaviour to be categorized as harassment. Other unwelcome behaviours are also prohibited if (i) they are based on an individual’s sex or gender (ii) are persistent or highly serious and (iii) create an atmosphere which is intimidating or hostile. These include but are not limited to lewd remarks or gestures, highly offensive jokes of a sexual nature, commenting inappropriately about another’s body, and stalking; e) Gender Discrimination: Adverse treatment of individuals based on their gender rather than on merit. This would include instances such as the singling out (for such adverse treatment as lower salary or grades, or more severe punishment) of person(s) on the basis of sex or gender. Mindful to the advanced era of information technology and social media platforms, much emphasis is made to all the actions categorized as harassment when done physically or verbally as it would also be considered as harassment when done electronically such as through the internet, e-mails, social media, texting, telephone, voicemail etc. In this very policy also, a concept of Inquiry Committee is in field making it responsible for the investigation and adjudication of any complaint received in connection with the violation of this policy. Reference can be made to: (https://www.hec.gov.pk/english/services/Documents/HARASSMENT-POLICY).

In the wake of above discussion, we are of the firm view that there was no justification apparently available to the learned Tribunal to modify the quantum of punishment awarded by the Competent Authority in the case, therefore, the CPLA.No.851-L/2024 is converted into an appeal and allowed. As a consequence thereof, the impugned order of the learned Tribunal dated 08.12.2023 is set aside and the penalty for forfeiture of past service of 05 years imposed by the Secretary, Government of Punjab Special Education Department, Lahore vide order dated 15.02.2022 is restored and the service appeal filed by the respondent/petitioner in the learned Tribunal is dismissed. So far as the CPLA.No.1379-L/2024 filed by the petitioner/respondents is concerned, it is otherwise barred by 174 days. Since the Government’s appeal against the same order is allowed and punishment awarded by the department has been restored therefore, this civil petition is dismissed and leave is refused.

Bearing in mind, the seriousness and sensitivity of the matter, the Office is directed to transmit the copy of this judgment to the Federal Secretary of the Ministry of Federal Education and Professional, Chief Secretaries and Secretaries of School and Higher Education of all the provinces, and the Federal Ombudsperson and the Provincial Ombudsmen to ensure the elimination of sexual harassment cases at grassroots level from all government and private educational institutions with meaningful measures and strict enforcement of Code of Conduct for Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace, ratified pursuant to Sections 2 (c) and 11 of the Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act 2010. Furthermore, directions ought to have been issued by an Office Order/Circular by the Ministry of Education (Federal and Provincial) to all the persons in command of government and private educational institutions for displaying the copy of Code of Conduct for Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace in English and other vernacular languages at conspicuous places and also issue directions to constitute an in-house “Inquiry Committee” as mandated in the aforesaid law in every government and private educational institution to deal with the cases of harassment so that an aggrieved lady teacher may submit her complaint promptly and directly to the inquiry committee rather than wholly and solely dependent upon mercy and hoping action by the head of institution on such complaint.
